description: The Teacher Re-Engagement Initiative is a scheme of the Department of Education of the state of Victoria for qualified teachers who stopped teaching at least a year ago, whether they retired or moved to another job. It lets them spend up to forty paid days in a public school to get used to the classroom again before they apply for a real post. After a teacher registers, a team from the department calls them, offers free coaching on writing a CV, preparing for interviews and the current curriculum, and finds them a school; during the forty days they observe lessons, teach and are guided by serving teachers. Those returning from retirement or a career break are paid up to 12,000 Australian dollars (about 7,200 euros) for the forty days. The initiative began in late 2022, received more than 1,100 expressions of interest in its first months and was given 12 million Australian dollars (about 7.2 million euros) in the 2023/24 state budget; placements ran until June 2025.

policy: Incentive pay for returning retired teachers (2020, made permanent) and ministerial letter campaign (2023)
description: Quebec pays retired teachers who come back to work in public schools much better than an ordinary substitute. From their first day of substitute teaching they are paid at the salary step they had reached when they retired, roughly 412 Canadian dollars a day (about 275 euros) instead of the usual substitute rate of 212 dollars (about 140 euros), and they keep their full pension. The measure was introduced on 21 September 2020, during the pandemic, brought 700 retirees back that school year and was later made permanent. In August 2023 the Minister of Education also wrote personally to every retired teacher inviting them to return; more than 5,000 retirees had worked in schools the previous year, mostly as substitutes or on part-time contracts, and the top daily rate was raised to 578 dollars (about 385 euros).

policy: Silver-Age Lecturing Plan: retired teachers posted to rural schools, 2018–
description: The Silver-Age Lecturing Plan sends retired teachers to work in poor rural schools. Retired principals, senior teachers and ‘special-grade’ teachers aged 65 or under apply to a call issued by their province and are posted for at least one school year to a rural primary or lower-secondary school, where they teach, coach the school's young teachers and advise the head on running the school. They keep their pension and receive an allowance from the central government of 20,000 yuan a year (about 2,500 euros) to cover a stipend, travel and insurance. The plan was launched in 2018 by the Ministries of Education and Finance with a target of 10,000 posts over three years; 7,000 teachers were recruited in the 2024 round alone, and in 2023 it was folded into a broader National Silver-Age Teachers Action Plan covering all levels of education.

policy: Higher, then no, earnings ceiling for retired teachers who keep teaching, 2022–2024
description: In Lower Saxony a retired teacher who went back to teaching used to lose part of the pension as soon as pay and pension together exceeded a ceiling set by the state's pension law. To make returning worthwhile, the state parliament raised that ceiling step by step: from 100 to 125 percent of the teacher's former pay in 2019, and to 150 percent from 1 October 2022 as part of a teacher-recruitment package, which allowed a pensioner to teach about nine or ten hours a week without any deduction. Overtime pay for serving teachers was raised by 15 percent at the same time. Since 31 October 2024 the ceiling for retired teachers has been abolished altogether, so they can now earn as much as they like from teaching while keeping their full pension.
secondary_instruments: Information & nudges (letters to teachers nearing retirement)

policy: Minister's letter to teachers approaching retirement (November 2023)
description: In November 2023 the Minister of Education of Lower Saxony, Julia Willie Hamburg, wrote a personal letter to every teacher who was about to retire. The letter thanks them for their years of service and asks them to keep helping the schools, which face rising pupil numbers, and it comes with an information sheet and a registration guide that explain the two ways of doing so: civil-servant teachers can ask to postpone their retirement by up to three years, and any teacher can retire and immediately be re-hired on a fixed-term contract while keeping the pension, thanks to the relaxed earnings rules described on the previous slide. The letter itself carries no money; it simply makes sure that every teacher knows the options before signing the retirement paperwork.

policy: Waiver of pension abatement for retired teachers: 50 days a year (2021–2027)
description: In Ireland a retired teacher who goes back to work normally sees the pension reduced whenever pension and new salary together exceed the pay they had when they retired, a rule known as abatement. To ease the shortage of substitutes, the Department of Education introduced a waiver in 2021: the first fifty days a retired teacher works in a calendar year, as a substitute or on a fixed-term contract, do not count for abatement, so the pension is paid in full. Every day worked counts as one day, however many hours it lasts, and only from the fifty-first day is the usual rule applied. The waiver was set out in a departmental circular in 2021 and has since been renewed twice, for 2024 and 2025 and again for 2026 and 2027.

policy: Abolition of the teacher licence renewal system (1 July 2022)
description: Between 2009 and 2022 a Japanese teaching licence expired every ten years unless the holder completed a thirty-hour renewal course, so teachers who had left the profession usually lost their licence and became what is known as ‘paper teachers’. In May 2022 the Diet amended the Educational Personnel Certification Act and the renewal system was abolished on 1 July 2022. Every licence that was valid on that date, including the dormant licences of people no longer teaching, became valid for life, with no procedure and no fee, which removed the main administrative barrier to returning. Boards of education have since built on this with seminars and consultation days for licence holders who left or never entered teaching, for example in Saitama, Chiba and Nagoya.

policy: Grant to primary schools for re-hiring former teachers, 2017–2020
description: Between November 2017 and January 2020 the Dutch Ministry of Education paid primary schools a grant for every former teacher they re-hired. A school board qualified if it hired a qualified teacher who had not worked in primary education for at least twelve months, on a contract of at least six months. The grant was up to 2,500 euros per returner and had to be spent on that person's guidance and support during the first months back, such as coaching or refresher training, so that both the teacher and the school found the return easier. The first round set aside 1.25 million euros, enough for 500 returners, and a further application round opened in 2019. The scheme is now closed.

policy: Streamlined return-to-teaching pathway: no refresher course, fees covered (2024–2028)
description: New Zealand has made it much simpler for a registered teacher who has been away from the classroom to get back the licence needed to teach, called a practising certificate. Teachers who had not taught for five years or more used to have to complete a Teacher Education Refresh course first. Now, if they have a job offer, they simply renew their certificate, can do substitute teaching for up to twenty half-days while the renewal is processed, and agree a short ‘Future-Ready Teaching Plan’ with the school principal instead of taking the course. Since October 2024 the Government has also paid the certificate fees of returning teachers, and 352 teachers had come back by April 2025. Budget 2025 extended this by covering all teacher registration fees and levies until June 2028, at a cost of 53.3 million New Zealand dollars (about 29 million euros).

policy: Decree-Law 51/2024: schools may hire retired teachers for shortage posts, 2024/25–
description: Since the 2024/25 school year Portuguese public schools have been allowed to hire retired teachers on fixed-term contracts to fill posts they cannot staff. A school with an unfilled post in a shortage subject, or a school officially classed as under-staffed, applies through an online form of the schools' administration directorate, and the ministry authorises the contract within a yearly quota agreed with the Finance ministry. Only teachers who retired five years ago or less can be hired. The retiree keeps the full pension and, on top of it, receives a payment linked to the first step of the teacher salary scale in proportion to the hours taught each week. The measure was created by a decree-law of 28 August 2024 as part of the government's ‘More Lessons, More Success’ plan against teacher shortages; according to the newspaper Público, 62 retirees were cleared to return in the first round.

Singapore's Ministry of Education keeps a register of former teachers whom schools can call on for short and flexible periods of work. Any trained ex-teacher, including retirees, who holds a teaching diploma from the National Institute of Education can register through the ministry's relief-employment portal; schools then contact them directly for appointments lasting from a single day to ten weeks, either for teaching only or for a mix of teaching and other duties agreed with the school. They are paid a daily rate and earn pro-rated leave after ninety days of cumulative service. A companion scheme offers former teachers contracts of one year to eighteen months. The ministry told Parliament in 2025 that between 2022 and 2024 about 220 teachers a year had joined the scheme within twelve months of leaving the service.

policy: Skolverket web-based training for returning teachers and preschool teachers (since 2018)
description: Sweden's National Agency for Education, Skolverket, runs an online refresher course for qualified teachers and preschool teachers who want to return to the profession after working elsewhere. It was built at the request of the Government and has been available on the agency's learning platform since October 2018. A returner logs in, chooses the track for schools or for preschools, and takes only the modules they need, in any order. The modules bring them up to date on the curricula, laws and official guidelines that changed while they were away, and a certificate is issued for each module completed. The course is open to anyone holding a Swedish teaching licence or a qualifying degree, and its purpose is to lower the threshold for the many trained teachers now working outside schools to come back.

policy: Re-entry counselling and induction for returning teachers (Zurich University of Teacher Education)
description: The Zurich University of Teacher Education, together with the school office of the Canton of Zurich, offers a package of advice and support for teachers who want to return to the classroom after a long break or after working in another field. It begins with a re-entry consultation and an assessment interview that checks whether returning makes sense and what preparation is needed; the first hour is free and the rest is subsidised by the canton. During the first school year back, a teacher who has been away for eight years or more can use the university's induction programme free of charge: up to twenty-five hours of mentoring by an experienced colleague at the school, individual and group supervision, coaching in their subject, and optional courses on grading, classroom management and working with parents.

policy: Return to Teaching Advisers (Department for Education)
description: Anyone who has taught or trained to teach in the United Kingdom and is thinking of coming back can ask the Department for Education for a free personal Return to Teaching Adviser through its ‘Get Into Teaching’ service. The former teacher calls or signs up online, and the adviser then works with them one to one, by phone, text or e-mail and for as long as they need: reviewing the skills they gained while away, helping them write applications and prepare for interviews, pointing them to refresher courses and professional qualifications, and alerting them to vacancies and webinars. The Department used the same channel in its ‘Come back to teaching’ campaign of January 2022. Returners are a major source of teachers in England: about 17,500 full-time-equivalent teachers came back in 2023, some 38 percent of all qualified entrants that year.

policy: House Bill 385: full-time return of retired teachers in high-need subjects (2022–2026)
description: Since 1 July 2022 the state of Georgia has let retired teachers go back to full-time classroom teaching in shortage subjects without giving up their pension. A teacher who retired with thirty or more years of service and has been retired for at least a year can be hired as a full-time teacher in one of the three subjects of greatest need in their region, typically special education, mathematics, science, English or elementary teaching, and receives a full salary on top of the full pension. The school district pays the pension contributions and the retiree earns no further pension rights. A state audit in 2025 found that about 350 retirees a year had used the law, less than one percent of Georgia's teachers. The law expires on 30 June 2026 and is being replaced by a new one, Senate Bill 150.

policy: Retired Mentors for New Teachers (Aurora Public Schools; REL Central evaluation, 2017)
description: Aurora Public Schools, a district in Colorado, pays recently retired teachers to mentor new teachers. Retired teachers with a strong record in the district are hired part-time to accompany first- and second-year teachers in high-poverty elementary schools for two years, meeting them every week and observing their lessons, which is far more support than the district's usual one-year ‘buddy’ scheme. For the retiree it is a paid, part-time way back into the school system; for the district it is a way to keep expertise in the classroom. A randomised trial run by the Regional Educational Laboratory Central for the US Institute of Education Sciences, published in 2017, followed 77 new teachers in 11 schools: it found a small gain in pupils' mathematics results after the first year that did not last, no effect on reading and no effect on whether the new teachers stayed.
